observation: Existing LLM-based multi-agent systems can handle simple dialogue tasks, but complex tasks remain difficult because naively chaining LLMs induces cascading hallucinations and logic inconsistencies. Real-world LLM agent frameworks tend to oversimplify the complexities of collaborative problem solving and often rely on unstructured natural-language dialogue, which loses information across rounds and produces unproductive chatter. Existing code-generation methods also lack self-correction mechanisms that verify runtime executability, leaving complex software engineering tasks unmet.

claims: Public code benchmarks such as HumanEval and MBPP contain function-level code tasks, unlike datasets that focus on real-world software engineering aspects.
On a seven-task SoftwareDev comparison, AutoGPT, LangChain, and AgentVerse obtain an average executability score of 1.0, failing to produce executable code, while ChatDev obtains 2.1.

In the statistical analysis on SoftwareDev, ChatDev has an executability of 2.25, consumes 19,292 tokens, generates 1.9 code files, 77.5 total code lines, 40.8 lines per code file, requires 762 seconds, and has a human revision cost of 2.5.
AgentVerse, like general-purpose agent frameworks, lacks the ability to systematically deconstruct requirements for complex software systems.

solution.idea: The recurring failure mode across existing frameworks is that they use natural-language dialogue as both the coordination medium and the verification medium. CAMEL, Mindstorms, ChatDev, and similar systems let one agent address another agent in free text; the receiving agent must infer state from an utterance that can be stale, ambiguous, or hallucinated. Because the only artifact that survives a round is text, the next agent's context is already contaminated. A separate but related failure is that code review is also performed by an LLM that has never run the code, so it can confidently approve code that does not import or passes only its own imagined tests. The proposed direction therefore separates the medium of collaboration from the medium of verification: agents communicate by reading and writing structured, versioned artifacts in a shared workspace; and code is accepted only after it has been executed against concrete tests in an isolated runtime. In this design, a deterministic controller, not an LLM, decides which agent acts next and when a loop must stop. LLM agents are reduced to specialized functions: one converts requirements into a structured specification, one decomposes that specification into a task graph, one implements a single graph node, and one repairs a node when an execution report shows a concrete failure. No agent sends a free-form message to another agent. The artifact produced by one stage is the only input passed to the next stage, and every artifact is a typed record with a version, an owner phase, and an explicit dependency on earlier artifact versions. This addresses cascading hallucinations because the context length of a downstream agent no longer grows with the number of dialogue rounds; it only contains the relevant current code, interface contract, and execution evidence. It also addresses unproductive chatter because all communication is constrained to mutations of the shared workspace, and the controller enforces a finite state machine over phases. The runtime verifier, rather than an LLM reviewer, supplies the ground truth for executability. Static, natural-language review may still be used for style or design suggestions, but it can never change a node's status from 'unverified' to 'verified'; that transition requires a pass report from the executing test harness. This principle directly answers the observation that code-generation systems lack self-correction grounded in runtime executability. In designing this solution, the alternative of retaining free-form dialogue and adding a separate test runner was considered. That alternative is rejected because the dialogue history still introduces drift, irrelevant messages, and repeated instructions, and because the actors doing repair would have no obligation to ground their statements in execution traces. A second alternative, replacing multi-agent decomposition with a single agent and an execution loop, was also considered. That alternative fails for complex software tasks because one agent cannot hold the full requirements, design, code, and test state in a reliable form; the problem needs an explicit shared project memory. The chosen design deliberately makes the protocol schema more rigid and requires an engineer to define artifact types for each application domain. This is an acceptable cost because the payoff is that no information is lost except by deliberate compaction of a specification, and no incorrect code can be hidden behind fluent language.
solution.implementation:
The implementation is organized around a deterministic controller, a typed shared workspace, and a small set of agent roles. The controller owns the state machine and invokes the appropriate LLM or tool. The controller also enforces all transition rules and termination criteria; it is not an LLM.

The shared workspace stores the following artifact types, each with an `artifact_id`, `version`, `created_by`, `timestamp`, and `parent_version` field. The primary artifact types are: `Specification`, `RequirementTree`, `PlanNode`, `CodeEntry`, `ExecutionRecord`, `IntegrationRecord`, and `IssueRecord`. A `Specification` contains a structured restatement of the user request: goal, input/output contracts, constraints, example calls, and acceptance criteria. The `RequirementTree` decomposes the specification into reusable requirements with identifiers. A `PlanNode` represents one code unit to be produced, and includes a `node_id`, `source_file`, `function_or_class_interface`, `depends_on` list of prerequisite node identifiers, `test_refs`, and `state`. The state of a `PlanNode` follows the sequence `untouched`, `implemented`, `compile_checked`, `runtime_checked`, and, after integration, `accepted`. A `CodeEntry` contains one full version of the source code for a single node, plus the node_id it implements and the version of the interface contract it was generated against. An `ExecutionRecord` captures the output of running that code: `phase` can be `compile`, `import`, `unit_test`, or `integration_test`; `status` can be `pass`, `fail_compile`, `fail_runtime`, `fail_assertion`, `timeout`, or `error`; and it stores the stdout, stderr, traceback, exception type, failing test name, expected value, actual value, and a precise diff if available. An `IssueRecord` is created only when an `ExecutionRecord` has status other than pass. It identifies the failing `node_id`, the `code_version`, the `execution_record_id`, the evidence type, and the repair attempt number. `IssueRecord` has no free-text field that can override execution evidence.

The agents are: `SpecAnalyst`, `Planner`, `Implementer`, and `Repairer`. `SpecAnalyst` receives the raw user text and outputs a `Specification` JSON object conforming to a strict schema. `Planner` receives the `Specification` and the `RequirementTree`, and returns a set of `PlanNode` objects. Decomposition is recursive: any `PlanNode` that is still too large is expanded into child nodes in the workspace before implementation begins. `Planner` must write public function signatures and expected behavior for each node so that tests can be attached before code exists. It also marks dependency edges. `Implementer` receives exactly one `PlanNode`, the generated interface contracts of its dependency nodes, the relevant portions of the `Specification`, and any test descriptions that already exist. It returns one `CodeEntry`. Crucially, the prompt to `Implementer` never includes previous dialogue, review comments, or another agent's personality. `Repairer` receives the failing `ExecutionRecord`, the current `CodeEntry`, the same `PlanNode` and dependency contracts, and the relevant test expectations. It returns a repaired `CodeEntry` and, optionally, a short human-readable explanation that is archived but not used as input to later agents.

The central self-correcting loop for one node is as follows. The controller collects all dependency nodes that have reached `accepted`, assembles their current `CodeEntry` versions, and invokes `Implementer` for the next node. When a new `CodeEntry` is available, the controller marks the node `implemented` and invokes the `RuntimeHarness`. The harness is not an LLM; it is a sandboxed container containing the available interpreter, the current collected code tree, and the test suite. The harness first checks that the source file can be parsed and imported. It then runs the tests listed in `test_refs`. These tests were written or derived from the `Specification` and `PlanNode` interface before the node was implemented, so they cannot be changed by `Implementer` or `Repairer` to make failures disappear. A test includes smoke tests for the required function or class, standard calls with expected outputs, and edge cases derived from the specification. The harness records an `ExecutionRecord` and stamps it with the exact `code_version`. If the record is not pass, the controller calls `Repairer`. The repair loop is allowed at most `MAX_REPAIR_ROUNDS`, a configurable integer, defaulting to 5. After each repair attempt the harness runs again and writes a new `ExecutionRecord`. When a pass record is obtained, the controller marks the node `runtime_checked`. This acceptance rule is strict: no comment from any LLM can set `runtime_checked`; the status changes only through an `ExecutionRecord` with status `pass`. A consequence is that an LLM reviewer, if used, is only allowed to attach a `suggestion` issue, and suggestions never prevent acceptance; they are queued for the next planned refactoring phase and must still be validated by the harness.

After all leaf nodes individually pass runtime tests, the controller enters the integration phase. It builds a single code tree from the accepted `CodeEntry` versions and runs the entire acceptance suite listed in the `Specification`. The integration harness generates an `IntegrationRecord` that covers inter-module behavior. If integration fails, the controller inspects the traceback in a purely mechanical way: it maps the failing file or imported symbol to the owning `PlanNode` using the task graph. It creates an `IssueRecord` for that node, but does not let a new `Repairer` simply declare the code fixed. It first determines whether the failure is caused by an interface mismatch between dependency nodes. If a dependency contract has changed, the controller invalidates the downstream nodes by resetting them to `untouched` and re-invokes `Planner` to update the interface. If the failure is within one node, the controller invokes `Repairer` with the integration traceback and the integration `ExecutionRecord`, then reruns the unit harness for that node and reruns the integration harness. This forms an outer loop that continues until the integration record is pass or until `MAX_INTEGRATION_ATTEMPTS`, another configurable integer, is reached. The design prevents infinite loops because every loop iteration is tied to a new artifact version and a counter, and because the controller, not an agent, decides when to escalate. Escalation creates an `EscalationRecord` that is routed either to a human operator or back to `Planner` with the requirement to reduce the scope of the current task.

Communication between agents is implemented through workspace reads and writes only. There is no message bus that delivers one agent's sentence to another agent. When an agent needs clarification, it does not ask a peer in dialogue; it writes a structured `ClarificationRequest` containing the artifact id, the ambiguous requirement id, and possible interpretations. `Planner` or `SpecAnalyst` is called by the controller to resolve that request by producing a new version of the affected artifact. This change makes the protocol finite and auditable. The controller tracks round counts with `repair_count`, `integration_attempt`, and `clarification_count`, and every agent output is parsed by a schema validator. If an LLM returns invalid JSON or a semantically incomplete artifact, the controller resubmits the same action with the validator error message, for at most two attempts; after two failures, the task is paused for human intervention. This addresses the observed pitfalls of assistant repeated instruction and infinite loops.

All prompts to LLM agents are rendered from structured artifact fields and pass through a template that uses the artifact's ID and version as the only context. Downstream prompt construction never concatenates previous exchanges. For example, the `Implementer` template contains only: current task text for the one node, the public interface, the relevant test descriptions, and the interface versions of dependencies. The `Repairer` template contains the failing `ExecutionRecord` with its traceback and test diff, plus the current code and contract. This controlled input allows runtime evidence to dominate the repair process. In addition, the system stores all past versions of every `CodeEntry` and `ExecutionRecord`, so if a later integration attempt reveals that an earlier fix removed a needed behavior, the controller can compare versions and hand the `Repairer` a diff between the older passing unit version and the newer failing integration version. The repair is then based on a concrete regression, not on an LLM's memory of what was said. The entire implementation consists of these five deterministic layers: artifact schemas, controller state machine, agent templates and output validators, runtime harness, and task-graph bookkeeping. This provides the missing self-correcting runtime verification and the structured, non-chatty collaboration that existing role-play and general agent frameworks under-specify.
